sources/de-vries-woude-first-modern-econ.title: de Vries & van der Woude — The First Modern Economy (1500–1815)
sources/de-vries-woude-first-modern-econ.content:
Jan de Vries and Ad van der Woude, The First Modern Economy: Success, Failure, and Perseverance of the Dutch Economy, 1500–1815. Cambridge University Press, 1997. The extracted text has 35,882 lines and about 2.4 MB of clean born-digital text. The book is the main quantitative economic history source in the wiki and argues that the Dutch economy was the first to exhibit the linked characteristics of modern economic growth. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Contents
The book is organised in three parts: Structures, Sectors, and Analysis. It combines geography, demography, money, taxation, agriculture, fishing, industry, foreign trade, social structure, wages, living standards, and macroeconomic interpretation into one long-run account from 1500 to 1815. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Part I — Structures (Ch. 1–5)

Ch. 1: By way of introduction — historiography of Dutch economic history, why the Dutch case matters for theories of sustained growth, and the authors’ aim of replacing older narrative/institutional traditions with a synthetic structural and quantitative account. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 2: Structures — geography, rivers and waterways, settlement patterns, the Little Ice Age, the international political environment, secular economic trends, land reclamation, communications, peat supplies, and environmental consequences. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 3: The people — regional population growth to 1795, differences between west/north/east/south, Batavian-French era population change, urbanization, migration, and population composition. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 4: Money and taxes, borrowing and lending — money supply, mint production, Habsburg and republican public finance, excise taxes, public debt, the Holland bond market, banking practices, the Amsterdam Wisselbank, commercial credit, insurance, merchant bankers, international capital markets, and efficient markets. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 5: Three questions — medieval legacy, whether there was a specifically Calvinist economy, and whether the dutch-republic formed a single national economy through internal trade and distribution. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]

Part II — Sectors (Ch. 6–10)

Ch. 6: Agriculture — early sixteenth-century agriculture, the 1500–1650 rise, 1650–1750 and 1750–1815 changes, agricultural output, yields, land use, rental prices, specialization, and productivity. Links: agriculture, polder-model-water-management, standard-of-living. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 7: Fishing — inland fishing, coastal fishing, herring, lesser fisheries, whaling, and conclusions about fishing as a specialized export and provisioning sector. Links: industry-and-manufacturing, naval-warfare-and-sea-power. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 8: Industry — textiles, new draperies, linen, cotton, silk, cotton printing, sail cloth, woodworking, shipbuilding, sawmilling, ceramics, brickworks, pottery, pipe making, paper, printing, brewing, distilling, tobacco, sugar refining, construction, and patents. Links: industry-and-manufacturing, leiden, amsterdam, rotterdam. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 9: Foreign trade until the mid-seventeenth century — early Dutch trade, the merchant ship, mid-sixteenth-century trade, crisis and expansion, Russia, Norway, Sweden, Italy, the Levant, the rise of the VOC, Africa, the New World, and merchant shipping at mid-century. Links: spice-trade, pre-company-expeditions, voc-finance-and-capital, colonial-empire. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 10: Foreign trade after the mid-seventeenth century — hegemony and crisis, grain, herring, salt, textiles, timber, Asian trade, VOC finances, domestic impact of the VOC, West Indian trade, slave trade, sugar/plantation economy, other growth sectors, and trade volume/value by region. Links: atlantic-empire-and-slavery, voc-finance-and-capital, colonial-empire. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]

Part III — Analysis (Ch. 11–14)

Ch. 11: City and country — urban-rural symbiosis, crafts, industry, occupational structure, nobility, rural people, city people, women and children, and income distribution in Holland cities. Links: urbanization, wages-and-labor, standard-of-living. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 12: Standard of living and labor market — nominal wages, cost of living, real wages, labor demand/supply, segmented labor market, exceptionality lost, income redistribution, and poor relief. Links: wages-and-labor, standard-of-living. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 13: The course of the economy — phases before the Revolt, the Golden Age economy, crisis and response after 1663, the eighteenth-century economy, final crisis 1780–1815, Malthusian model, merchant capitalism, the first-modern-economy thesis, national-income estimates, and Dutch/British per-capita comparison. Links: dutch-republic, public-finance, england. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Ch. 14: Postlude — long-run framing of success, failure, and perseverance across the early modern and Napoleonic-era economy. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]

Coverage Guide

Core thesis — the Dutch Republic as a first modern economy: high productivity, urbanization, market orientation, public finance, capital markets, commercial specialization, and high wages. Links: dutch-republic, urbanization, public-finance, standard-of-living. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Geography and infrastructure — rivers, waterways, communications, peat, land reclamation, environmental constraints, and the constructed landscape of the Golden Age economy. Links: polder-model-water-management, agriculture, amsterdam, rotterdam. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Population and cities — regional growth, migration, the West/North/East/South divide, high urbanization, city-country symbiosis, and occupational structure. Links: urbanization, leiden, haarlem, amsterdam, delft. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Money, taxation, and credit — excises, public debt, Holland’s bond market, the Wisselbank, insurance, merchant bankers, and international capital flows. Links: public-finance, amsterdam-exchange-bank, voc-finance-and-capital, dutch-republic-power-structure. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Productive sectors — agriculture, herring, whaling, textiles, shipbuilding, sawmilling, brewing, sugar refining, printing, and construction. Links: agriculture, industry-and-manufacturing, dutch-cartography-and-atlases, spice-trade. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Foreign trade and empire — Baltic and European trades, Levant trade, VOC rise and profitability, West Indian trade, slave trade, plantation economy, and post-1650 trade by region. Links: voc-dutch-east-india-company, colonial-empire, atlantic-empire-and-slavery, spice-trade, new-netherland-and-new-amsterdam. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Social outcomes — income distribution, labor markets, women and children, poor relief, wages, real wages, and cost of living. Links: wages-and-labor, standard-of-living, religion-and-politics. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Decline and persistence — crisis after 1663, eighteenth-century adjustment, final crisis after 1780, and comparisons with later British leadership. Links: dutch-republic-timeline, england, anglo-dutch-rivalry. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]

Data and Tables
The book contains over 90 tables across all chapters. Key table clusters include population by province and city; money supply and mint output; Holland public debt from 1599 to 1796; Wisselbank deposits from 1609 to 1820; land reclamation; agricultural output, yields, and land use; herring and Sound volumes; VOC financial results before and after 1650; Leiden textile output; wage and cost-of-living series from 1500 to 1815; income distribution in sixteen Holland cities; Dutch national-income estimates; and Dutch/British per-capita comparisons. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
High-Value Passages to Mine

Introduction and thesis passages on the Netherlands as the first country to achieve sustained economic growth. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Land reclamation, waterways, peat, and communication passages for polder-model-water-management and the geographic foundations of growth. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Public debt, excise taxation, Wisselbank, insurance, and capital-market passages for public-finance and amsterdam-exchange-bank. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Agriculture, herring, shipbuilding, textiles, brewing, printing, and sugar refining passages for sector pages. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
VOC financial results, domestic VOC expenditure, West Indian trade, slave trade, and plantation-economy passages for empire pages. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]
Wage, cost-of-living, real-wage, labor-market, income-distribution, and poor-relief passages for living-standard pages. ^[source: raw/de-vries-woude-first-modern-economy.txt]

Useful For

dutch-republic, dutch-republic-power-structure, and dutch-republic-timeline as the economic spine of the Republic.
agriculture, urbanization, industry-and-manufacturing, wages-and-labor, and standard-of-living for domestic structure and social outcomes.
public-finance, amsterdam-exchange-bank, and voc-finance-and-capital for credit, debt, banking, and capital markets.
colonial-empire, atlantic-empire-and-slavery, spice-trade, and voc-dutch-east-india-company for the economic side of empire.

The raw file is an EPUB-derived text rather than a page-marked PDF transcription, so it is excellent for thematic mining and keyword search but less useful for exact page citation unless checked against the printed edition.

sources/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-du.title: Jorink — Reading the Book of Nature in the Dutch Golden Age, 1575-1715
sources/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-du.content:
Jorink — Reading the Book of Nature in the Dutch Golden Age, 1575-1715
Eric Jorink’s Reading the Book of Nature in the Dutch Golden Age, 1575-1715 is a study of natural history, natural philosophy, theology, and learned culture in the seventeenth-century dutch-republic. It argues that many Dutch investigators understood nature as a second book of God alongside Scripture, and that collecting, observing, describing, and representing natural objects remained deeply religious and metaphysical activities even amid Cartesian and post-Cartesian scientific change. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Coverage
The source covers the Dutch interpretation of the Book of Nature from the late sixteenth century into the early eighteenth century. Its chapters move from the older metaphor of nature as a legible divine book to Cartesian disruption, comet debates, insect studies, curiosity cabinets, and books of wonders. The source is the strongest current base for the wiki’s intellectual/scientific layer. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
The book’s cast includes Constantijn Huygens, Christiaan Huygens, Gisbertus Voetius, René Descartes, Baruch Spinoza, Balthasar Bekker, Jan Swammerdam, Antoni van Leeuwenhoek, Frederik Ruysch, Bernardus Paludanus, Nicolaes Witsen, Albertus Seba, Levinus Vincent, and Dutch poets, theologians, collectors, publishers, and naturalists who used the language of wonder, reading, observation, and divine order. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Contents

Chapter 1: Introduction — frames the Dutch Golden Age within Scientific Revolution historiography and challenges a purely mechanistic or secularized reading of Dutch science. It places Stevin, Huygens, Swammerdam, Leeuwenhoek, Descartes, Spinoza, and later historians inside a broader question: how did Dutch learned culture interpret nature? ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Chapter 2: The interpretation of the Book of Nature — traces the two-books metaphor, Scripture and creation, Genesis, exegesis, poetry, natural theology, and debates over how nature could be read without undermining the Bible. Links: book-of-nature, religion-and-politics, philosophy. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Chapter 3: Comets: the debate on the wonders in the heavens — treats comets as prodigies, natural phenomena, signs, and contested objects of interpretation from before 1660 into debates around 1700. It connects astronomy, providence, orthodox theology, Cartesian explanation, and public controversy. Links: scientific-revolution, dutch-natural-philosophy, philosophy. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Chapter 4: Insects: the wonders of God in the humblest creatures — follows classical and humanist traditions into microscopic and anatomical insect study, with jan-swammerdam central to the transformation of the Book of Nature. It also includes antoni-van-leeuwenhoek, Stephan Blankaart, collectors, and insect curiosity around 1700. Links: scientific-revolution, book-of-nature, dutch-natural-philosophy. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Chapter 5: Collections of curiosities: from the Book of Nature to naturalia — covers Dutch curiosity collections down to around 1660, Bernardus Paludanus, Nicolaes Witsen, Frederik Ruysch, Albertus Seba, Levinus Vincent, and the shift from mixed cabinets of curiosities toward cabinets of naturalia. Links: curiosity-cabinets, dutch-knowledge-culture, china-trade, spice-trade. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Chapter 6: Books of wonders — follows printed wonder literature, natural-historical books, representations of marvels, and the persistence of wonder around 1700. It is useful for connecting printing, collecting, images, theology, and natural history. Links: dutch-knowledge-culture, dutch-cartography-and-atlases, scientific-revolution. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]

Coverage Guide

Book of Nature theology — the source repeatedly treats nature as a readable divine book paired with Scripture. This supports the wiki’s explanation of why observation, description, and collecting could be religious acts rather than secular departures from religion. Links: book-of-nature, religion-and-politics, philosophy. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Cartesianism and anti-Cartesian response — Cartesian mechanism matters, but Jorink presents it as one benchmark within a larger Dutch culture of exegesis, wonder, Reformed orthodoxy, and natural theology. Links: dutch-natural-philosophy, philosophy, scientific-revolution. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Comets and interpretation — comets show how Dutch authors negotiated prodigy, providence, natural causation, astronomy, and public controversy. Links: scientific-revolution, religion-and-politics. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Insects and microscopy — insects, microscopes, Swammerdam, Leeuwenhoek, and Blankaart provide concrete cases where close observation intensified rather than erased wonder. Links: jan-swammerdam, antoni-van-leeuwenhoek, scientific-revolution, book-of-nature. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Curiosity cabinets and global objects — collections connect Dutch trade, travel, specimens, shells, animals, preparations, books, display, and learned prestige. Links: curiosity-cabinets, dutch-knowledge-culture, colonial-empire, spice-trade. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Printed knowledge and wonder — books of wonders, illustrations, catalogues, poetry, and natural histories make the Dutch Republic’s knowledge culture a printed and visual culture as well as an experimental one. Links: dutch-cartography-and-atlases, art-market, dutch-knowledge-culture. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]

High-Value Passages to Mine

Introduction passages on the Scientific Revolution in the Netherlands and the limits of a purely mechanistic/secular story. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Chapter 2 passages on the two books, Genesis, literal reading, exegesis, and the sanctioning of the Book of Nature by Scripture. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Cartesian/Voetius/Spinoza/Bekker passages for future expansion of philosophy or a dedicated Dutch Cartesianism page. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Comet passages for an event/concept page on signs, prodigies, and natural explanation in Dutch public culture. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Swammerdam, Leeuwenhoek, and insect passages for microscopy, anatomy, reproduction, generation, and the theology of small creatures. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Paludanus, Ruysch, Witsen, Seba, and Vincent passages for future collector/entity pages and for curiosity-cabinets. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]

Value for the wiki
This is a high-value source for the wiki’s intellectual and scientific layer. It supports philosophy, scientific-revolution, dutch-natural-philosophy, book-of-nature, and curiosity-cabinets, and adds detail on how Dutch Golden Age science coexisted with Reformed theology, biblical exegesis, wonder, collections, microscopy, and global objects supplied through trade. ^[source: raw/jorink-reading-book-of-nature-dutch-golden-age.txt]
Useful Themes

The Book of Nature as a shared metaphor across poets, theologians, naturalists, and collectors.
Cartesianism as an important but incomplete benchmark for Dutch scientific culture.
Orthodox Reformed resistance to philosophies that seemed to separate nature from Scripture.
Comets, insects, microscopes, and cabinets as sites where wonder, observation, and theology overlapped.
Dutch collections of naturalia and curiosities as an interface between books, objects, commerce, and learned display.
Printed wonder, catalogues, illustrations, and natural-historical books as part of the Republic’s knowledge infrastructure.

sources/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.title: Koeman — Joan Blaeu and his Grand Atlas (1970)
sources/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.content:
Dr. Ir. C. Koeman, Joan Blaeu and his Grand Atlas. George Philip & Son Limited / Theatrum Orbis Terrarum, 1970. The extracted raw text has 3,655 lines and about 180 KB of clean text. It is the wiki’s main source for joan-blaeu, the House of Blaeu, the Atlas Maior, and the material production of Dutch Golden Age cartography. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Contents
Koeman treats the Atlas Maior as both a cartographic achievement and a social object of the Dutch Golden Age. The preface stresses that the atlas reflected high contemporary cartography, engraving, printing, binding, papermaking, Amsterdam commercial capacity, and patrician display; it was not a popular object but a costly artifact for elite owners, diplomatic gifts, and learned libraries. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]

Preface — frames the Atlas Maior as a monument of the Golden Age: cartographic knowledge, luxury craft, Amsterdam publishing scale, and elite display amid the wars, disease, poverty, and uncertainty of seventeenth-century life. Links: dutch-republic, amsterdam, dutch-knowledge-culture, art-market. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Ch. 1: Biography of Joan Blaeu — Joan’s birth in Alkmaar, youth in amsterdam, Leiden education, father Willem Jansz Blaeu as globe-maker, instrument-maker, printer, pupil of Tycho Brahe, the Damrak shop, family religion, marriage, public offices, Amsterdam civic status, and rivalry with Janssonius. Links: joan-blaeu, amsterdam, leiden. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Ch. 2: Printing house and cartographical institute — the Blaeu works on the Bloemgracht and Gravenstraat, letterpress and copperplate presses, type, paper, engraving, map printing, colouring, bindings, stock catalogues, workforce estimates, and the workshop as a combined printing house, map factory, and commercial publishing office. Links: industry-and-manufacturing, dutch-cartography-and-atlases, amsterdam. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Ch. 3: Origin and growth of Blaeu’s Atlas — Willem Blaeu’s maritime and atlas publications, pilot books, the Light of Navigation, the Appendix, the 1635 world atlas, the father-to-son expansion, catalogue evidence, acquisitions of plates, and competition with Hondius/Janssonius. Links: dutch-cartography-and-atlases, petrus-plancius, jan-huygen-van-linschoten. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Ch. 4: The Atlas Maior — the 1662 Latin edition and French, Dutch, German, and Spanish forms; the giant folio format; more than six hundred hand-coloured maps; about 3,000 pages of text; printing calculations; editions and surviving copies; luxury bindings; display cabinets; and use as diplomatic or company gifts. Links: dutch-knowledge-culture, dutch-republic, voc-dutch-east-india-company. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Ch. 5: The cartographical contents of the Grand Atlas — a region-by-region survey of maps for Europe, the Netherlands, Asia, Africa, and America, including sources, plate histories, copied and older maps, omissions, and the limits imposed by confidential VOC material. Links: dutch-cartography-and-atlases, china-trade, new-netherland-and-new-amsterdam, colonial-empire. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Ch. 6: The fire of 22 February 1672 — the fire in the Gravenstraat printing house, destroyed stock, type, presses, copperplates, and the blow to the atlas enterprise. Links: dutch-republic-timeline, amsterdam, joan-blaeu. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Ch. 7: Further history of the Atlas Maior — surviving copies, later ownership, facsimile history, catalogues, variants, and the atlas’s afterlife as a collector and library object. Links: dutch-knowledge-culture, dutch-cartography-and-atlases. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Appendix and notes — extant-copy documentation, edition details, map plate evidence, catalogue references, and bibliographic apparatus. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]

Coverage Guide

Joan Blaeu as person and civic figure — the source gives the strongest current biographical spine for joan-blaeu: family, Amsterdam childhood, Leiden education, marriage, civic offices, religious sympathies, reputation, and death after the 1672 fire. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Amsterdam print capitalism — Koeman details the Blaeu workshop as a large production system: presses, copperplates, type, paper, engravers working offsite, map colouring, bookbinding, catalogues, and roughly eighty workers at peak production. Links: amsterdam, industry-and-manufacturing, dutch-knowledge-culture. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Atlas as luxury and diplomacy — the Atlas Maior functioned as patrician display, expensive library furniture, state gift, VOC/States-General diplomatic gift, and high-status artifact. Links: art-market, dutch-republic, voc-dutch-east-india-company, dutch-knowledge-culture. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Map knowledge and secrecy — the regional content chapter shows both cartographic abundance and constraint: Blaeu reused older plates and sources, omitted some available American material, and could not publish confidential VOC coastal charts by Johannes Vingboons. Links: dutch-cartography-and-atlases, colonial-empire, new-netherland-and-new-amsterdam, china-trade. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Blaeu versus Janssonius/Hondius — the source is useful for the competitive atlas market, plate acquisition, copying, rivalry, and how commercial pressure shaped the growth of Dutch world atlases. Links: dutch-cartography-and-atlases, amsterdam. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Disaster and decline — the 1672 fire provides a concrete event connecting the Rampjaar environment, business vulnerability, and the collapse of a major Amsterdam cartographic enterprise. Links: dutch-republic-timeline, joan-blaeu, amsterdam. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]

Illustrations and Visual Material
The volume includes plates of Blaeu printer’s marks, title pages, portraits of Willem Jansz and Joan Blaeu, maps of Europe and the world, an interior of a map-printing house, the printing house on the Bloemgracht, the East India House, illustrations from the Light of Navigation, Gerard Hulft, a manuscript chart on vellum, a printed vellum chart by Pieter and Joan Blaeu, the second printing house, Joan Blaeu’s house, the Townbook of Italy, a contemporary cabinet with the Atlas Maior, Chekiang from the Chinese Couplet-Witsen atlas, maps of the Netherlands and Holland, and a scheme of Blaeu atlas production. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
High-Value Passages to Mine

Preface passages on the Atlas Maior as Golden Age monument, elite object, and product of Amsterdam commercial capacity. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Biography passages on Willem Jansz Blaeu’s Amsterdam shop, Tycho Brahe connection, Joan’s Leiden years, civic status, religious sympathies, and rivalry. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Printing-house passages on presses, copperplates, stock rooms, engravers, map printing, colouring, binding, and workforce scale. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Atlas Maior production passages on editions, map counts, text volume, hand-colouring, luxury bindings, owners, and diplomatic gift copies. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
Regional map-content passages for the Netherlands, Asia, Africa, America, Brazil, New Netherland, China, and confidential VOC chart material. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]
1672 fire passages for the destruction of plates, type, stock, and the later history of the firm. ^[source: raw/koeman-blaeu-grand-atlas.txt]

Useful For

joan-blaeu as a person, printer, publisher, cartographer, and Amsterdam civic figure.
dutch-cartography-and-atlases as the main source for Blaeu atlas production and map content.
dutch-knowledge-culture for the link between commerce, printing, collecting, display, and geographical knowledge.
amsterdam, industry-and-manufacturing, and art-market for luxury production and urban craft organization.
colonial-empire, china-trade, and new-netherland-and-new-amsterdam where atlas maps and VOC secrecy intersect imperial knowledge.

Quality
Born-digital text, clean and fully readable. Minor form-feed artifacts and occasional OCR spacing remain from PDF conversion. The source is compact but dense, especially for production history, editions, map contents, visual plates, and the 1672 fire.

sources/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.title: Masselman — The Cradle of Colonialism (1963)
sources/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.content:
George Masselman, The Cradle of Colonialism. Yale University Press, 1963. The extracted raw text has 23,836 lines and about 1.2 MB of readable OCR from a scanned copy. It is the wiki’s strongest narrative source for Dutch corporate colonialism in Southeast Asia, centered on the VOC, jan-pieterszoon-coen, the spice monopoly, batavia, the english-east-india-company, john-jourdain, bantam, Ambon, and Banda. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Contents at a Glance
Masselman presents Dutch colonialism as a modern corporate form of empire rooted in capital investment, private enterprise, monopoly rights, and the East Indies spice trade. The preface argues that the Dutch, rather than the Portuguese, Spanish, or English, first converted overseas capital investment into a durable colonial-commercial system in the East Indies; English failure in East Asia redirected English attention toward India. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
The book has three large movements. Book I explains the Dutch background: delta geography, sea labor, herring, Baltic and Iberian trade, Amsterdam, the Revolt, capital formation, merchant organization, Linschoten, Plancius, Arctic attempts, and the first Cape voyages. Book II follows the pre-company rush to Asia, the political creation of the VOC, early operational failures, Portuguese/Asian trade background, and the company’s first experiments with armed monopoly. Book III becomes a long Coen-centered narrative: biography, English rivalry, Coen’s imperial program, Jacatra/Batavia, Banda, English withdrawal, free-trade disputes, and the post-Coen consequences of monopoly colonialism. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Full Contents Map
Book I — The Background


Ch. 1: The Land and the People — Opens from the Dutch physical environment: peat-digging, lakes, erosion, the “water-wolf,” salt/fuel problems, drainage, dikes, and the constant double struggle against water and land loss. Masselman uses geography as causal background, not scenery: scarcity of land and fuel, vulnerability to flooding, and the discipline of water management help explain why the Dutch became technically practical, commercially restless, and maritime. Mine this chapter for polder-model-water-management, agriculture, and the material foundations of dutch-republic. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 2: The Sea — Moves from the land to the sea economy, especially fishing, herring regulation, curing, packing, town marks, crews, and the institutional supervision of quality. The chapter treats maritime labor as a school for seamanship and as a commercial system linking North Sea fishing, ship handling, provisioning, salt demand, and export discipline. Useful for connecting naval-warfare-and-sea-power with industry-and-manufacturing and with the later ability to staff long-distance fleets. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 3: The Sea Lanes Become Longer — Traces the northward movement of European trade centers from Bruges to Antwerp and then toward Amsterdam, emphasizing silting waterways, Scheldt access, wool, the Hansa, Iberian connections, and the broadening range of Dutch shipping. The chapter is about how Dutch commerce outgrew local waters before the Indies: Baltic carriage, Iberian salt and wine, Antwerp’s rise and fall, and the geographic logic that made Holland and Zeeland middlemen between northern and southern Europe. Mine for amsterdam, antwerp, urbanization, and the pre-Asian roots of Dutch carrying trade. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 4: The Town — Focuses on Amsterdam as civic-commercial machine: protected harbor on the IJ, access through the Zuiderzee, inland connections, municipal development, trade privileges, urban government, migration, religious change, and the 1578 Alteration. Masselman describes the town as a platform where merchants, magistrates, refugees, Calvinists, and trade infrastructure combined; Amsterdam becomes not simply a port but the institutional environment from which overseas ventures could be financed and organized. Use for amsterdam, dutch-republic-power-structure, public-finance, and urbanization. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 5: Independence at Any Price — Places overseas expansion inside the Revolt: Spanish pressure, Parma, Leicester, Calvinist agitation, merchant-magistrates, war finance, and the conflict between religious zeal and commercial survival. The chapter shows the Dutch fighting for independence while still needing trade with enemy-linked markets, creating a persistent tension between God, country, and profit. It is useful background for religion-and-politics, william-of-orange, philip-ii-of-spain, johan-van-oldenbarnevelt, and the later logic of state-backed commerce. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 6: Factors of Trade Expansion — Explains why Dutch trade expanded during war instead of collapsing: Mediterranean ventures, herring growth, salt shortages, Cape Verde salt, Guinea, African coasts, shipbuilding, low freight rates, insurance, credit, and the willingness to enter risky markets. Masselman emphasizes practical pressures—salt, fish, shipping, routes, capital, and enemy exclusions—as forces pushing the Dutch from European trade into Atlantic and Asian opportunity. Mine for public-finance, naval-warfare-and-sea-power, amsterdam-exchange-bank, and the economic preconditions of voc-finance-and-capital. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 7: From Guilds to Capitalism — Presents the organizational transition from medieval guild restraint to joint ventures, outside investment, limited risk, divided shares, and early stock-company forms. The chapter is one of the best places in the source for Masselman’s capitalism thesis: the Indies trade required more capital than single merchants could risk, and Dutch practice made pooled investment normal before the VOC made it permanent. Use for voc-finance-and-capital, voc-governance, public-finance, and the broader “cradle of colonialism” argument. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 8: Three Merchants and a Minister — Introduces the Amsterdam men and networks behind the Asian turn: Hendrik Hudde, Reynier Pauw, Balthasar de Moucheron, Petrus Plancius, and the commercial-religious refugee world that carried intelligence, capital, and anti-Iberian zeal. The chapter links merchants, Calvinist exile, navigation, map knowledge, and Amsterdam politics; it is a bridge between domestic urban history and concrete preparations for the Indies. Mine for petrus-plancius, amsterdam, dutch-cartography-and-atlases, and possibly a future Reynier Pauw page. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 9: Linschoten and His Itinerary — Gives the route-intelligence chapter: jan-huygen-van-linschoten, his Portuguese service, information on Goa, Madagascar, the Indian Ocean, Portuguese weakness, sailing directions, Japan, China, and how the Itinerario broke the Iberian information monopoly. Masselman treats Linschoten as a converter of secret imperial experience into publishable Dutch commercial knowledge. Use this chapter heavily for pre-company-expeditions, portuguese-in-asia, dutch-cartography-and-atlases, and dutch-knowledge-culture. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 10: North to the Indies — Covers the first serious Northeast Passage planning: Plancius, Moucheron, Barentsz, Oldenbarnevelt, the States of Holland and Zeeland, the Kara Sea, Novaya Zemlya, and the assumption that a northern route to Cathay/Cipango might bypass Iberian power. The chapter is as much about political-commercial coordination as about exploration; it shows provincial bargaining and merchant ambition shaping geographic experiment. Use for arctic-exploration, petrus-plancius, johan-van-oldenbarnevelt, and Dutch route strategy before the Cape route won. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 11: South to the Indies — Narrates the first Dutch Cape-route voyage: Houtman, Plancius’s instructions, ship fitting, councils of navigators and merchants, Cape/Madagascar route problems, Bantam, pepper, internal quarrels, violence, limited profit, and proof of possibility. Masselman makes this a messy experimental voyage rather than a heroic breakthrough: navigational knowledge was incomplete, command was divided, and the return mattered because it proved Dutch ships could reach Asian markets. Mine for houtman-brothers, pre-company-expeditions, bantam, spice-trade, and early company governance problems. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 12: The Second and Third Voyages North — Returns to Arctic attempts after the first southern voyage, covering state support, Hakluyt’s manuscript, Moucheron, the States-General, Barentsz, Novaya Zemlya, and the slow death of the northern-route dream. The chapter is useful because it shows that the Cape route did not immediately eliminate northern hopes; Dutch expansion developed through competing route projects before commercial results selected the southern passage. Use for arctic-exploration, pre-company-expeditions, and the interaction of English geographic intelligence with Dutch planning. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Book II — The East India Company


Ch. 1: Amsterdam Collects — Follows the second southern voyage and the gathering of knowledge from Houtman’s failures: better routing around the Cape, Plancius’s advice, stronger leadership, Van Neck, Heemskerck, Bantam, Ambon, Ternate, Banda, and Portuguese weakness. The chapter shows Amsterdam learning from error and converting a disappointing first voyage into a more profitable, systematic venture. Mine for pre-company-expeditions, bantam, spice-trade, portuguese-in-asia, and Amsterdam’s role as organizer. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 2: The Rush to the Indies — Describes the explosion of competing voyages in 1598–1602: Amsterdam, Zeeland, Moucheron, Van Neck, Heemskerck, English intelligence through John Davis, Bantam pepper shortages, overbuying, inter-Dutch rivalry, and the beginning of market self-damage. This is the key chapter for why consolidation became necessary: too many Dutch companies chased the same spices, bid up Asian prices, and risked dumping returns in Europe. Use for pre-company-expeditions, english-east-india-company, bantam, and voc-finance-and-capital. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 3: The Prime Mover of the United Company — Narrows to political pressure for merger, especially Oldenbarnevelt and the States’ interest in preventing Dutch competitors from ruining each other while war with Spain continued. The chapter also includes the capture of the Portuguese carack and the emergence of kraak porcelain as proof that armed seizure and Asian luxury trade could produce spectacular returns. Use for johan-van-oldenbarnevelt, voc-governance, dutch-republic-power-structure, china-trade, and the political origin of VOC unity. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 4: The Formation of the United East India Company — Gives the detailed institutional story of the 1602 VOC charter: Amsterdam versus Zeeland, Oldenbarnevelt’s mediation, chambers, directors, the Seventeen, monopoly rights, state powers, capital commitments, duration, and the balance between provincial jealousy and unified policy. This is the source’s central chapter for VOC structure. Mine it for voc-dutch-east-india-company, voc-governance, voc-finance-and-capital, amsterdam, and the States-General’s delegation of warlike powers to a company. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 5: By Trial and Error — Shows the early VOC discovering that monopoly on paper did not solve Asian realities: Portuguese resistance, English rivalry, Ceylon/Kandy, Achin, Ambon, Banda, factories, instructions, uncertain alliances, and the practical problem of enforcing purchases over enormous distances. The chapter is useful for the gap between corporate design in the Netherlands and operational improvisation in Asia. Use for portuguese-in-asia, voc-asian-headquarters, malacca-and-malay-world, spice-trade, and early factory policy. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 6: War and Trade Do Not Mix — Develops the title’s problem through Van der Hagen, Matelief, Goa, Calicut, Ambon, Banda, Bantam, Portuguese fleets, and the costs of using armed expeditions to secure trade. Masselman shows that warfare might open ports or damage Portuguese power, but it also consumed capital, delayed returns, confused commercial priorities, and exposed the company to local-political complexity. Mine for voc-governance, naval-warfare-and-sea-power, portuguese-in-asia, banda-extirpation, and the trade/war tension that later Coen tried to resolve by territorial command. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 7: The Seventeen Under Attack — Covers the VOC’s first domestic crisis: falling share prices, pepper gluts, failed attacks on Portuguese strongholds, criticism of the Seventeen, Isaac Le Maire, Lyntgens, political complaints, and shareholder pressure. The chapter is excellent for showing that the VOC was contested from the start, not an immediately successful machine. Use for voc-governance, voc-finance-and-capital, amsterdam, and the early Dutch securities-market story. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 8: 1607: The Burgeoning Year — Treats 1607 as a turning point across several fronts: Dutch religious refuge for English separatists, Oldenbarnevelt, Spanish negotiations, Heemskerck and Gibraltar, Matelief, Ternate, Asian expansion, and the broader confidence of the Republic. In VOC terms, the chapter marks movement from defensive, uncertain ventures toward more assertive sea power and Asian treaty-making. Use for voc-1607-turning-point, naval-warfare-and-sea-power, religion-and-politics, and portuguese-in-asia. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 9: Early Asiatic Trade: the Hindu Period — Provides deep Asian background rather than Dutch narrative: Van Leur’s trade model, commenda-style finance, monsoon shipping, small cargoes, active traveling merchants, passive investors, Hindu-Buddhist polities, Vijaya, Kertanagara, Chinese contact, and pre-European Southeast Asian trade. This is one of the best chapters for preventing a Eurocentric reading of the VOC: Masselman sketches the commercial world Europeans entered rather than created. Use for asian-trade-before-europeans, india-textile-trade, malacca-and-malay-world, and java-and-mataram. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 10: Background in Asia — Continues Asian context through Islam, Chinese and Japanese trade, Turkish/Ottoman pressure on older routes, Venice/Genoa, Malacca, Java, Sumatra, the spice islands, and the political-commercial environment of Southeast Asia before Dutch dominance. The chapter explains why Europeans came by sea and why control over choke points, ports, rulers, and monsoon routes mattered. Mine for malacca-and-malay-world, java-and-mataram, china-trade, japan-trade, spice-trade, and asian-trade-before-europeans. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 11: The Portuguese Age — Summarizes the Estado da India: Vasco da Gama’s arrival, Calicut and the Samorin, Muslim merchant opposition, fortresses, naval violence, Goa, Malacca, Hormuz, Macao, Portuguese administrative weakness, corruption, crusading claims, and limits of trade organization. Masselman uses the Portuguese as both precedent and contrast: they built armed positions in Asia, but not the Dutch form of capitalized corporate monopoly. Use for portuguese-in-asia, malacca-and-malay-world, china-trade, and VOC displacement of Iberian networks. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Book III — Jan Pieterszoon Coen


Ch. 1: Jan Pieterszoon Coen — Begins Coen’s biography: baptism in Hoorn, family background, father Pieter Willemszoon van Twisk, Hoorn’s commercial world, the adoption/use of the Coen name, early schooling, the town’s maritime-commercial environment, and later Italian training. The chapter is useful for seeing Coen as product of Dutch provincial merchant culture rather than as an isolated imperial genius. Mine for jan-pieterszoon-coen, Hoorn context, and the personnel background of voc-governance. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 2: The Bottom of the Ladder — Follows Coen’s entry into VOC service at low rank, fleet mustering, recruitment, sailors, soldiers, low wages, harsh shipboard conditions, mixed crews, and the path by which ambitious young men could rise inside the company. Masselman uses the chapter to describe the labor ecology of the VOC: skilled officers, underpaid servants, waterfront recruits, soldiers, discipline, disease, and mortality. Use for voc-shipboard-life, voc-governance, voc-dutch-east-india-company, and Coen’s early institutional formation. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 3: Coen’s First Contact with the Indies — Covers Coen’s first Asian experience under Verhoef: Portuguese encounters, Calicut, Banda, Bandanese negotiations, Dutch violence and vulnerability, English presence, Bantam, and the lessons Coen drew from fragmented trade, weak authority, and treacherous alliance politics. This chapter is important because it provides the experiential foundation for Coen’s later insistence on centralized command and coercive monopoly. Mine for jan-pieterszoon-coen, banda-extirpation, bantam, portuguese-in-asia, and voc-monopoly-system. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 4: The English versus the Dutch — Steps back to compare English and Dutch economic development before the EIC/VOC clash: wool, staples, Bruges, cloth, monarchy, London, English frustration, Drake, royal support, and the relative Dutch advantage in European carrying trade. Masselman is setting up the rivalry by explaining why England felt both entitled and late in Asian commerce. Use for england, london, english-east-india-company, anglo-dutch-rivalry, and Dutch-English structural comparison within existing concept pages. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 5: The English East India Company — Gives the EIC’s early institutional and financial context: Elizabethan chartering, London merchants, undercapitalization, intermittent voyages, English pride, weak sustained support, and the contrast with Dutch scale. The chapter is especially useful for why the English could challenge but not displace the VOC in the spice islands. Mine for english-east-india-company, london, england, spice-trade, and the English side of anglo-dutch-rivalry. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 6: A Servant of the English Company — Biographical chapter on john-jourdain: family and will details, Old Style/Gregorian date issues, his voyage from Woolwich, English company service, Ascension, Middleton, Hawkins, Portuguese opposition, factory life, quarrels among English servants, and Jourdain’s experience before becoming Coen’s counterpart. This is the strongest single source section for a full Jourdain page. Mine it for john-jourdain, english-east-india-company, anglo-dutch-rivalry, and the personnel culture of English Asian trade. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 7: Up the Ladder — Brings Coen and Jourdain into direct rivalry as Coen rises: Coen’s return to Holland, promotion to chief merchant, reports to the Seventeen, Bantam, Ambon, Luhu, Kambela, clove competition, English-Dutch price escalation, and Coen’s growing authority. The chapter shows Coen moving from talented servant to strategist and Jourdain emerging as the English obstacle. Use for jan-pieterszoon-coen, john-jourdain, bantam, anglo-dutch-rivalry, and amboyna-massacre background. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 8: Blueprint for Empire — Centers on Coen’s programmatic vision: Dutch colonies, offensive strategy, planted settlers, strong fleets, control of Asian trade, use of Portuguese colonial precedent, and the argument that trade could not be secured by scattered factories alone. This is the key chapter for Coen’s imperial ideology and for the transition from company trade to company empire. Mine for voc-asian-headquarters, voc-monopoly-system, colonial-empire, jan-pieterszoon-coen, and the territorial logic behind batavia. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 9: The Rendezvous — Explains the practical problem Coen wanted to solve: the need for a fixed Asian rendezvous and command center. It covers Bantam, Djakarta/Jacatra, Mataram, Gerard Reynst, inter-Asian capital needs, return-cargo financing, local rulers, and the limits of running the Indies from dispersed factories. This is a core chapter for voc-asian-headquarters, batavia, bantam, java-and-mataram, and the financial geography of the VOC in Asia. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 10: The Price of Monopoly — Shows monopoly becoming coercive policy: decrees against native trade, ultimata to coastal princes, Ambon/Banda/Malacca/Solor, English interference, Coen’s contract logic, confiscation, and the claim that monopoly rights justified restricting other Asian traders. The chapter is crucial for the moral and practical cost of VOC spice control: free trade disappears under the needs of exclusive supply. Use for voc-monopoly-system, spice-trade, banda-extirpation, anglo-dutch-rivalry, and colonial-empire. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 11: Second in Command — Covers Coen under Laurens Reael and the internal politics of VOC command: low salaries, temptation of private gain, European family absence, servants, soldiers, discipline, Reael’s more conciliatory policy, Coen’s disagreement, and the problem of enforcing company aims through imperfect personnel. The chapter is valuable for the contrast between Coen’s hard-line monopoly and Reael’s softer approach. Mine for voc-governance, jan-pieterszoon-coen, voc-shipboard-life, and internal VOC administrative culture. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 12: The Final Rung — Narrates Coen’s elevation to Governor-General amid tensions with Reael, the Seventeen, English/French competition, Bantam, and Dutch expectations. It shows why the directors chose Coen despite his abrasive tone: he had clarity, discipline, and a plan for making the VOC’s Asian system profitable and defensible. Use for jan-pieterszoon-coen, voc-governance, bantam, anglo-dutch-rivalry, and the lead-up to the Jacatra crisis. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 13: 1618 — Presents Coen in command and pressing the Seventeen for courage, ships, capital, and scale. The chapter shows him arguing that parsimony ruined great enterprises, sending laden ships home, preparing for confrontation in Java, and seeing himself as executor of a larger design than ordinary trade. Mine for jan-pieterszoon-coen, voc-finance-and-capital, voc-asian-headquarters, and the language of VOC imperial will. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 14: The Crisis — Covers the immediate crisis with Bantam, Djakarta/Jacatra, and the English: Jourdain’s appointment as principal English agent, London capital, English decision to stand firm, Coen’s exposed position, Dale, Widjaja Krama, and the diplomatic-military compression that made Jacatra decisive. This is one of the best chapters for the English-Dutch-Javanese triangle before Batavia. Use for anglo-dutch-rivalry, john-jourdain, english-east-india-company, bantam, batavia, and java-and-mataram. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 15: The Siege — Reconstructs the siege of the Dutch fort at Jacatra through the roles of Djakarta, Bantam, and the English rather than through heroics. Masselman stresses the local ruler’s desire to control his own town, Bantam’s jealousy of Djakarta’s trade, English opportunism, Dutch isolation, internal command problems under Van den Broecke, and the uncertain survival of the VOC position before Coen’s return. Mine for batavia, bantam, java-and-mataram, anglo-dutch-rivalry, and the prehistory of Batavia’s foundation. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 16: The Birth of an Empire — Narrates Coen’s return, storming and destruction of Djakarta, burning of the dalem and mosque, withdrawal of enemies, and the decision to establish the long-desired rendezvous as Batavia. This is where Masselman’s narrative turns from trade crisis to territorial founding: a VOC fort becomes a Dutch city and legal-political base in Java. Use for batavia, jan-pieterszoon-coen, voc-asian-headquarters, bantam, and colonial-empire. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 17: Steps Toward Consolidation — Details the building of Batavia as a VOC jurisdiction: Court of Justice, ordinances, tolls, Chinese taxes, arrack, leaseholds, plots, law and order, penalties, English tolls, and the assertion that the company now held Dutch territory in Asia. It also follows the effect of the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of Defense reaching Asia and complicating Coen’s victory. Mine for batavia, voc-asian-headquarters, voc-governance, china-trade, and Coen’s transformation of company factory into colonial state. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 18: The Conquest of Banda — Covers Coen’s Banda campaign, Bandanese resistance, Dutch military occupation, depopulation, forced control of nutmeg production, and the violent enforcement of exclusive contracts. Masselman treats Banda as the clearest case of monopoly colonialism becoming conquest: the spice islands are reorganized for company supply rather than local trade. Use for banda-extirpation, voc-monopoly-system, spice-trade, jan-pieterszoon-coen, and the darker side of colonial-empire. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 19: The English Withdrawal — Describes the weakening English position after the Treaty of Defense, capital shortage, inability to sustain the required fleet share, pullback from eastern spice competition, and the contrast between London hesitation and VOC infrastructure at Batavia. Coen reads English weakness as vindication of his hard line, while the Seventeen and States-General still have diplomatic constraints. Mine for english-east-india-company, anglo-dutch-rivalry, england, london, batavia, and the path toward English concentration on India. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 20: Monopoly or Free Trade? — Presents the policy dispute after Coen’s first governorship: Coen’s warning not to yield to English or French demands, the Seventeen’s instructions, States-General diplomacy, questions of private/free trade, and the tension between national interest, company rights, and European alliances. This is the main chapter for the ideological conflict between monopoly and open commerce inside Dutch policy. Use for voc-monopoly-system, voc-governance, spice-trade, anglo-dutch-rivalry, and public-finance. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Ch. 21: Mission Accomplished — Concludes Coen’s program with Batavia under threat from Mataram and Sultan Agung, Surabaya and Javanese politics, Batavia’s survival, Coen’s second governorship, and his sense that the essential framework of the VOC Asian empire had been established. The chapter is useful for linking Coen’s maritime-commercial project to inland Javanese power and to the defense of Batavia. Mine for batavia, java-and-mataram, jan-pieterszoon-coen, voc-asian-headquarters, and the early limits of Dutch power on Java. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Epilogue — Pulls the argument together: the Dutch came for spices, began with free enterprise, discovered that long-distance armed trade required heavy capital and coordination, and then created monopoly structures that damaged native trade, producers, company servants, stockholders, and spice-producing societies. Masselman contrasts Dutch corporate colonialism with Spanish/Portuguese conquest and crusade, emphasizing that commercial monopoly produced its own form of empire and impoverishment. Use for colonial-empire, voc-dutch-east-india-company, voc-monopoly-system, spice-trade, and synthesis on the costs of Dutch empire. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Afterword: Three Men — Profiles Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, Hugo Grotius, and Reynier Pauw as the Dutch-side architects and interpreters of the system Coen built in Asia. Oldenbarnevelt appears as political broker of the VOC and later victim of Dutch domestic conflict; Grotius as legal/intellectual defender of Dutch seizure and maritime claims; Pauw as Amsterdam power figure linking municipal interests, commerce, and company politics. Mine for johan-van-oldenbarnevelt, philosophy, amsterdam, voc-governance, and a possible future page on Reynier Pauw or Grotius as VOC jurist. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Coverage Guide


Corporate colonialism thesis — Masselman is the wiki’s key narrative source for how private capital, state privilege, monopoly rights, and violence produced a modern company empire. The strongest chapters are the preface, Book I Ch. 7, Book II Ch. 4, Book III Ch. 8, Ch. 10, Ch. 16–18, Ch. 20, and the Epilogue. Links: voc-dutch-east-india-company, voc-governance, voc-finance-and-capital, colonial-empire. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Dutch maritime and commercial background — Book I Ch. 1–7 connects geography, sea labor, herring, shipping, Baltic/Iberian trade, Amsterdam, war, capital, and guild-to-capitalist transition to overseas expansion. Links: polder-model-water-management, naval-warfare-and-sea-power, urbanization, public-finance. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Route knowledge and first voyages — Book I Ch. 8–12 and Book II Ch. 1–2 cover Linschoten, Plancius, Arctic voyages, Houtman, Van Neck, Heemskerck, Bantam, pepper, Portuguese information, and early failures/successes. Links: jan-huygen-van-linschoten, petrus-plancius, houtman-brothers, pre-company-expeditions, bantam. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


VOC formation and early structure — Book II Ch. 3–8 covers pre-company competition, Oldenbarnevelt, consolidation, monopoly charter, chambers, directors, shareholder attack, war/trade tension, and the 1607 turning point. Links: voc-governance, voc-finance-and-capital, dutch-republic-power-structure, voc-1607-turning-point. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Asian trade before and around European entry — Book II Ch. 9–11 gives the best source-page map for Hindu, Muslim, Chinese, Japanese, Southeast Asian, Ottoman, Venetian, and Portuguese contexts. Links: asian-trade-before-europeans, malacca-and-malay-world, india-textile-trade, java-and-mataram, portuguese-in-asia. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Coen as architect — Book III Ch. 1–3 covers Coen’s background and first Indies experience; Ch. 7–13 shows his rise and program; Ch. 14–18 shows crisis, Batavia, and Banda; Ch. 19–21 shows English withdrawal, free-trade dispute, and completion. Links: jan-pieterszoon-coen, batavia, voc-asian-headquarters, voc-monopoly-system. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Anglo-Dutch rivalry in Asia — Book III Ch. 4–7 and Ch. 14–20 are the strongest sections for English structural weakness, Jourdain, Bantam, Ambon/Banda competition, treaty politics, English withdrawal, and the road to Amboyna. Links: english-east-india-company, john-jourdain, anglo-dutch-rivalry, amboyna-massacre, england, london. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


Banda and monopoly consequences — Book III Ch. 10, Ch. 18, Ch. 20, and the Epilogue are the strongest mining areas for depopulation, forced production, extirpation of trees, passes, patrols, destroyed native trade, Ambon/Ternate/Tidore/Bantam decline, and monopoly impoverishment. Links: banda-extirpation, voc-monopoly-system, spice-trade, colonial-empire. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]


High-Value Passages to Mine

Preface passages defining Dutch East Indies colonialism as capital-investment colonialism and explaining why English failure in East Asia redirected English attention toward India. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Book I Ch. 1–7 passages on polders, sea walls, herring regulation, shipping, Baltic/Iberian trade, Amsterdam, war finance, merchant capital, and the guild-to-capitalist transition. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Book I Ch. 8–12 and Book II Ch. 1–2 passages on Linschoten, Plancius, Houtman, Van Neck, Heemskerck, Arctic voyages, Bantam, and route intelligence. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Book II Ch. 3–4 passages on Oldenbarnevelt, VOC formation, chambers, the Seventeen, monopoly rights, political mediation, and capital structure. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Book II Ch. 7 passages on Isaac Le Maire, shareholder attack, pepper glut, falling share prices, and early VOC governance criticism. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Book II Ch. 9–11 passages for Asian trade before Europeans and for Portuguese strengths/weaknesses that shaped Dutch strategy. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Book III Ch. 4–7 and Ch. 14–20 passages for Jourdain, the English East India Company, Bantam, English capital weakness, and direct Anglo-Dutch rivalry. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Book III Ch. 8–13 passages for Coen’s blueprint: colonies, rendezvous, monopoly, required capital, and the move from scattered factories to centralized Asian command. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Book III Ch. 15–17 passages for Jacatra siege, destruction of Djakarta, founding of Batavia, Dutch law, tolls, Chinese taxes, and Court of Justice. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]
Book III Ch. 18 and Epilogue passages for Banda, monopoly violence, native trade destruction, impoverishment, and the costs of spice control. ^[source: raw/masselman-cradle-of-colonialism.txt]

Useful For

Quality
Google Books OCR from a UC Berkeley library scan. Readable throughout with usual OCR artifacts: garbled section-header markers, fragmented words, odd spacing, page-number noise, and occasional misread names. Text density is high: about 23,800 lines across 564 scanned pages. The OCR is strong enough for source-page expansion and thematic mining, but exact quotations should be checked against the scan when precision matters.
